plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) weight loss in the randomized trials. SURMOUNT-1 averages for each dose arm vs placebo (adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks), how much results varied between people, why people with type 2 diabetes lost less on average (SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial), the share of loss that was lean mass, and the habits linked to getting the most from it. This is the fixed re-render of the held 11-16 script (playbook queue #3).
plan.angle: Keep the angle as written, with one change to the SURMOUNT-2 chapter. Phrase it as: 'In SURMOUNT-2, a separate 72-week trial in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, average weight loss was smaller than in SURMOUNT-1. The trials weren't head-to-head, and researchers have suggested possible reasons, but the trial wasn't designed to show why.' Don't state any cause as fact. Every number keeps one estimand, named once ('counting everyone who started'), including the share reaching 20% or more.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Weight Loss: How Much in Trials?
plan.target_keyword: how much weight can you lose on mounjaro
plan.why: Playbook queue #3 and the analyst's first priority. It's a broad, heavily searched question with momentum rising across 4 snapshots (80→84) ahead of the January surge, and it rests fully on NEJM trial data. | fact-check: This is a sound, evergreen pillar topic and the fix list for the 11-16 hold is complete. There is one framing problem. SURMOUNT-2 shows that adults with obesity or overweight AND type 2 diabetes lost less on average. It does not show why. The proposed reasons are hypotheses, for example lower starting weight, glucose-lowering medicines or differences in diabetes physiology. Stating any of them as a finding would claim a cause the trial doesn't support. Other checks for the content stage: (1) Use one estimand throughout. 'Counting everyone who started' means the treatment-regimen estimand. The ≥20% figures need to come from the same estimand, or be labelled if they come from the efficacy estimand. The NEJM abstract reports ≥20% for the 10 and 15 mg arms only; the 5 mg figure is in the tables. (2) Mounjaro label figures must be labelled as type 2 diabetes trials (SURPASS) and never set next to SURMOUNT-1 as if the two were compared directly. (3) The real-world Diabetes & Metabolism paper gets one context line at most, labelled observational, and only if its PubMed record is confirmed. (4) Protein advice keeps the kidney caveat, and the strength-training line says 'recommended', with no claim that it preserves muscle on tirzepatide unless a source shows it.

package.pinned_comment: In SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), 50% and 57% of people on the 10 mg and 15 mg tirzepatide arms lost 20% or more of their body weight over 72 weeks, vs 3% on placebo. Depending on dose, 9–15% on tirzepatide didn't reach a 5% loss. These are trial arms, not a dosing plan. In SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, averages were smaller. A trial's spread doesn't tell any one person where they'll land. Save this for your next appointment. If you're ever thinking about stopping, plan it with your prescriber. Don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.target_keyword: how much weight can you lose on mounjaro
script.hook_pattern: Open loop. Sentence 1 is a direct 'you' question that names tirzepatide. The headline average is spoken by about 10 s and a second number lands at 15–30 s. A one-sentence loop (what happened when people switched to placebo) pays off in the last chapter.

scenes.narration: If you're on tirzepatide or thinking about it, how much weight could you actually lose?
scenes.retention_device: Direct question hook: names the drug and the title's question in 'you' terms

scenes.narration: Short answer: on the top tirzepatide dose in the SURMOUNT-1 trial, average weight loss over 72 weeks was 20.9 percent of body weight. On placebo, over the same 72 weeks, it was 3.1 percent.
scenes.retention_device: Headline answer delivered by about 10 s

scenes.narration: Those were adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. And the SURMOUNT-1 averages here count everyone who was randomly assigned, whether or not they stayed on treatment.

items: Obesity, or overweight + a weight-related condition
visual.stock_query: diverse adults in clinic waiting room

scenes.retention_device: Scope and estimand named once, so every later SURMOUNT-1 number can be trusted

scenes.narration: Second number. Depending on dose, 85 to 91 percent of people on tirzepatide lost at least 5 percent of their body weight. On placebo, 35 percent did.

visual.stat_label: Lost 5%+: tirzepatide by dose vs placebo
visual.stock_query: crowd of people, most highlighted green

scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff at 15–30 s (Exp H)

scenes.narration: And stay with me, because later you'll see what happened to the weight when people in another trial were switched to placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, one sentence, paid off in 'What if you stop?'

scenes.narration: Quick label note first. In the US, tirzepatide is sold as Zepbound to reduce excess weight in certain people with obesity or overweight, and as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes. In the UK and some other countries, Mounjaro is also licensed for weight management.

visual.stock_query: two medicine boxes, one shared molecule

scenes.retention_device: Clears up the brand confusion behind the search term, for US and UK viewers

scenes.narration: So whichever brand name you search, the weight-loss answers come from tirzepatide's SURMOUNT trials.
So what did each dose actually do in SURMOUNT-1?
Here's the ladder, averaged over 72 weeks. On 5 milligrams, weight loss was 15 percent.

visual.stock_query: first step of a ladder glowing

scenes.narration: On 10 milligrams, 19.5 percent. On 15 milligrams, 20.9 percent. And on placebo, 3.1 percent.

visual.stock_query: bar chart ladder, placebo bar small

scenes.narration: These are trial arms, not a dosing plan. Which dose is right for you is your prescriber's call.
scenes.on_screen_text: Trial arms, not a dosing plan
scenes.retention_device: Trust beat: keeps the viewer safe

scenes.narration: The trial was big: 2,539 adults, randomly assigned to a tirzepatide dose or placebo, with a 72-week treatment period. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
Imagine Rosa, 50. She's hypothetical, but you might know her. A few months into tirzepatide, a friend at work seems to be losing faster, and Rosa quietly wonders if she's doing it wrong.
If you've had that thought, you're not alone. And one trial detail changes how Rosa should read that headline number.

visual.stock_query: Medi holding a hidden detail card

scenes.narration: Everyone in SURMOUNT-1, placebo group included, got regular lifestyle counselling. The aim was about 500 fewer calories a day and at least 150 minutes of physical activity a week.
So the 3.1 percent on placebo wasn't people doing nothing. It was diet and activity support, with placebo injections instead of tirzepatide.

visual.fact: Placebo got diet and activity counselling too

scenes.narration: That means the gap between the arms is roughly what tirzepatide added on top of that support.
scenes.retention_device: Reframe that makes the numbers click

scenes.narration: To make it concrete, here's arithmetic, not a promise. Someone starting at 220 pounds who lost 20.9 percent would lose about 46 pounds.
But an average is just the middle of a crowd. And in this trial, the crowd was spread out.

visual.stock_query: crowd spread across a wide field

scenes.narration: So will your result look like the average?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, person beside bell curve

scenes.narration: Not necessarily. On the 10 and 15 milligram doses, 50 and 57 percent of people lost 20 percent or more of their body weight.
On placebo, 3 percent reached that mark. That's about 1 in 33.

visual.stock_query: one person highlighted in big crowd

scenes.narration: Flip that around, and 43 to 50 percent of people on those doses lost less than 20 percent.
And at the far end, 9 to 15 percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, didn't reach a 5 percent loss.

visual.stock_query: small group at edge of chart

scenes.retention_device: Honest surprise: not everyone responds the same

scenes.narration: Here's another way to see it. On placebo, with counselling alone, 35 percent still lost at least 5 percent.
Same medicine, same trial, same counselling, and results ranged from very large to small. SURMOUNT-1 reported that spread. It doesn't tell any one person where they'll land.

visual.stock_query: scatter of dots on a board

scenes.narration: For Rosa, that's a relief. Her friend's pace isn't her yardstick. Her own trend over months, and how she's feeling, are what's worth bringing to her prescriber.

visual.stock_query: relieved woman smiling at her notes

scenes.narration: And weight is one health measure among many. Blood pressure, energy and blood sugar count too.
But there's one group where the average itself came out lower, and it's worth knowing if that's you.
What if you have type 2 diabetes? Imagine Rosa's brother, who does. His answer comes from a different trial.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, brother and sister talking

scenes.retention_device: Chapter opens with a question; thread extends

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-2, a separate 72-week trial in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, average weight loss was smaller than in SURMOUNT-1.

visual.stock_query: separate trial folder on its own desk

scenes.narration: On 10 milligrams, average loss was 12.8 percent. On 15 milligrams, 14.7 percent. On placebo, 3.2 percent.
The trials weren't head-to-head, and SURMOUNT-2 wasn't designed to show why the averages differed.
So if you live with diabetes and your numbers look smaller than a headline you saw, that doesn't mean you're failing. The headline came from a different trial, in different people.

One safety point for this group. If you have diabetes and take insulin or a sulfonylurea, the risk of low blood sugar is higher with tirzepatide, so your prescriber may need to review those medicines.
scenes.on_screen_text: Insulin or sulfonylurea? Low sugar risk

scenes.narration: And Mounjaro's own label reports results from type 2 diabetes trials that focused on blood sugar. They weren't set up to compare with SURMOUNT-1, so I'm keeping them apart.
Next comes the question people almost whisper. How much of the weight lost was muscle?
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: open loop into next chapter

scenes.narration: Was it fat, or muscle?
In a body-scan substudy of 160 SURMOUNT-1 participants, fat mass fell by 33.9 percent on tirzepatide, all doses combined.

visual.stat_label: Fat mass drop, tirzepatide all doses vs placebo, 160-person substudy

scenes.narration: On placebo, fat mass fell by 8.2 percent. Roughly a third, against about a twelfth.
Of the weight lost on tirzepatide in that substudy, roughly three-quarters was fat and about one-quarter was lean mass.
That's 160 people, not the whole trial, so treat it as a snapshot. But it's a good reason to look after the muscle you have.
scenes.on_screen_text: A snapshot, not the whole trial

visual.stock_query: camera snapshot of a small group

scenes.narration: Here's what US guidelines recommend for adults in general: at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days.
To be clear, SURMOUNT-1 didn't test whether strength training protects muscle on tirzepatide. It's recommended for adults in general, and that includes people on tirzepatide.
Protein matters too, but the right amount differs from person to person. If you have kidney disease, ask your prescriber or a dietitian before you eat more protein.

visual.stock_query: dietitian with plate of eggs, beans

scenes.narration: Imagine Rosa adding two short strength sessions a week. Not to chase the scale, but to feel steady on the stairs and strong carrying the shopping.
Before the result I promised you, there's one trade-off you deserve to hear about.
What did people put up with?
scenes.on_screen_text: What did people put up with?

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-1, the most common side effects on tirzepatide were stomach-related: nausea, diarrhea and constipation.
Most were mild to moderate, and they happened mainly while the dose was being stepped up.
Side effects led some people to stop treatment. That was about 4 to 7 percent on tirzepatide, depending on dose. On placebo, 2.6 percent.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for side effects, by dose vs placebo

scenes.narration: If you get severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain? Get help right away

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't stop or change it alone

scenes.narration: And if vomiting or diarrhea leaves you losing fluids, sip fluids unless you've been told to limit fluids, and tell your prescriber. The label warns that fluid loss from these side effects has been linked to kidney problems.

visual.stock_query: glass of water on bedside table

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to the question I left open at the start.
scenes.retention_device: Signals payoff of the main loop

scenes.narration: What happens when the medicine stops?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, road splitting in two

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-4, people switched to placebo after 36 weeks on tirzepatide saw their body weight rise by 14 percent on average over the next 52 weeks.

visual.stat_label: Weight change after switch to placebo, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: People who stayed on tirzepatide lost a further 5.5 percent over the same 52 weeks.

visual.stat_label: Further loss staying on tirzepatide, 52 weeks

scenes.narration: That trial randomized 670 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes: 335 stayed on tirzepatide and 335 switched.
And here's the twist people miss. Even the placebo group still ended 9.9 percent below their weight at the very start of the trial.

visual.stat_label: Placebo group, below starting weight, 88 weeks

scenes.narration: So in this trial, keeping the weight off was tied to staying on treatment, and some of the loss held even after switching.
If you're ever thinking about stopping, plan it with your prescriber. Don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
For Rosa, that turns 'how fast?' into a better question: what can I keep doing, for the long run?
Here's what to take with you.

One. In SURMOUNT-1, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, lost 15 to 20.9 percent of body weight on average by tirzepatide dose over 72 weeks. On placebo, 3.1 percent.

visual.stat_label: SURMOUNT-1 by dose vs placebo, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: Two. In SURMOUNT-2, a separate trial in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, averages were smaller. And in SURMOUNT-1, results on tirzepatide ranged from under 5 percent to over 20 percent.

visual.stock_query: checklist item two, spread of dots

scenes.narration: Three. In SURMOUNT-4, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, weight went back up on average after switching to placebo. So ask your prescriber about the long-term plan.
And bring these questions to your next appointment: what's a realistic range for me, how do I protect my muscle, and what's our plan for the long run?

factcheck.summary:
This script is accurate and safe. It can ship as written, and the two minor wording fixes below are optional but recommended.

**What I checked against sources**
- **SURMOUNT-1 numbers all match:**
  - 2,539 adults randomised.
  - Average loss at 72 weeks: 15.0%, 19.5% and 20.9% by dose vs 3.1% on placebo.
  - Lost at least 5%: 85–91% vs 35%.
  - Lost 20% or more: 50% and 57% vs 3%.
  - Stopped for side effects: 4.3–7.1% vs 2.6%.
  - Side effects were mostly mild to moderate.
  - The derived figures are correct: 43–50% lost under 20%, 9–15% lost under 5%, and 220 lb × 20.9% ≈ 46 lb.
- **SURMOUNT-2:** 12.8% and 14.7% vs 3.2% over 72 weeks, in adults with type 2 diabetes. Matches.
- **SURMOUNT-4:** 670 people randomised; −5.5% for those who stayed on vs +14.0% after the switch to placebo. Matches.
- **US labels:**
  - Zepbound (revised 8/2026): 5.3 "Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion" and 5.7 Hypoglycemia both exist.
  - Mounjaro: indicated for blood-sugar control in type 2 diabetes. The low-blood-sugar risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea is in the label.
- **Other sources:** the MHRA approval for weight management (8 Nov 2023) and the US physical activity guidelines page (last updated 19 Nov 2025) both check out.

**Checked from memory only**
- I couldn't load the PubMed pages, so I confirmed the three trial records through Europe PMC instead.
- Four details aren't in the abstracts I could open. I confirmed them from my knowledge of the papers, not from a page:
  - SURMOUNT-4: 335 per arm and the placebo group ending 9.9% below starting weight.
  - SURMOUNT-1: the 160-person body-scan figures (fat mass down 33.9% vs 8.2%, and the roughly 3:1 fat-to-lean split).
  - SURMOUNT-1: side effects happening "mainly while the dose was being stepped up".

**Framing and safety**
- Each finding keeps its trial population, comparison group and timeframe, and the recaps keep that scope.
- The script says plainly that the trials weren't head-to-head and calls the body-scan result a snapshot.
- All the required safety lines are there: the stomach-pain emergency line, the "don't stop or change your medicine" line, the fluids caveat, the low-blood-sugar caveat, the kidney-disease protein caveat and the "talk to your doctor" line.
- Rosa is clearly introduced as hypothetical.
- The subscribe and watch-next lines are allowed in a long-form video.

issues.claim: 2,539 adults, randomly assigned to a tirzepatide dose or placebo, all followed for 72 weeks.
issues.problem: Not everyone finished: some people stopped treatment or dropped out. 'All followed for 72 weeks' overstates it slightly, and s03 already says the averages include people who didn't stay on treatment.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "The trial was big: 2,539 adults, randomly assigned to a tirzepatide dose or placebo, with a 72-week treatment period. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine."

issues.claim: researchers have suggested possible reasons, but the trial wasn't designed to show why
issues.problem: It's tagged S2, but I haven't confirmed which sentence in the SURMOUNT-2 paper says this. The rule is to tag a line only after finding the sentence that says it.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "The trials weren't head-to-head, and SURMOUNT-2 wasn't designed to show why the averages differed." Keep on_screen_text "Not head-to-head; cause unknown" and source S2.

issues.claim: S4: 'Warnings: Acute Kidney Injury (5.3)'; S5: 'Warnings: Hypoglycemia' (no section number)
issues.problem: Minor title accuracy. Section 5.3 of the Zepbound label is titled 'Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion', and the S5 title gives no section number.
issues.fix: Change the S4 title to "Zepbound (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information: Indications (1); Warnings: Acute Kidney Injury Due to Volume Depletion (5.3), Hypoglycemia (5.7)". Check the hypoglycemia section number in the current Mounjaro PI and add it to the S5 title.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates keep the actual weight-loss numbers out of the thumbnail, so none trips the 'gives the answer away' cap, and all have decent legibility at phone size with a single clear focal point. #0 ('WILL YOU MATCH IT?') pairs most directly with the title's implicit question ('how much weight can you lose') by making it personal and self-relevant — the viewer wants to know if their own result would match the trial's, which is a strong, honest curiosity gap tied tightly to the title. The worried/surprised scale-face icon reinforces tension without contradicting the text. #1 ('72 WEEKS') is clean and legible but answers a tangential question (trial duration) rather than the title's actual promise (amount of weight lost), slightly weakening the curiosity hook. #2 ('FAT OR MUSCLE?') is a clever twist but pivots the hook away from 'how much weight' toward body composition, which risks feeling like a different video's thumbnail and could mildly mislead relative to the title. On balance, #0 has the strongest, most title-aligned curiosity gap with excellent legibility, making it the best choice.

issues.problem: With no subtext, 'IT' has nothing to refer to for a viewer who only sees the thumbnail. It's not misleading, just vague. The video's section is 'Will you match the average?'
